summaries.gardner: Marathon Petroleum is the opposite of a Rule Breaker: it is the top player in a mature, shrinking US refining industry with no emerging-industry tailwind or hard-to-copy innovation. It does show one Gardner trait, strong price momentum (shares up about 160% in 52 weeks to $478.07), and some commentators view the rally as stretched, but the business itself fails most of the six traits.
summaries.buffett: MPC is a simple business Buffett could understand, run by managers who return most cash to owners (diluted shares fell from 649M in 2020 to 306M in 2025, plus a $4.00 annual dividend). But it sells a commodity with weak pricing power, earnings swing with crack spreads (a $9,826M loss in 2020, $14,516M profit in 2022, $4,047M in 2025), and at about 16.6x trailing earnings near a cyclical peak there is no margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger would see a capably run commodity processor whose fortunes depend mainly on crack spreads it cannot control, which he generally avoided. Inverting, the ways it could fail include a long decline in gasoline demand, regulation and a margin collapse after the 2026 supply shock, though its scale and hard-to-replicate assets make outright failure unlikely.
summaries.lynch: Lynch would class MPC as a cyclical, and his rule for cyclicals is to buy when earnings are depressed and P/E looks high, not after a spike; Q2 2026 EPS of $17.73 versus $3.96 a year earlier and a 160% one-year share gain suggest it is late in the cycle. The story is easy to tell and the buybacks are big, but consensus sees revenue falling about 11% in 2027.
summaries.fisher: MPC fails most of Fisher's growth tests: it has little R&D, few new products beyond renewable diesel and MPLX gas expansion, and sales have fallen from $177,453M in 2022 to $132,699M in 2025. It scores better on operations, cost control (refining costs of $5.72 per barrel in Q2 2026) and candid reporting.
summaries.graham: MPC is large and pays dividends, but it fails Graham's defensive tests: it lost money in 2020, has paid dividends only since its 2011 spin-off, trades at about 30x its 2023-2025 average EPS of $15.64, and its P/E times P/B of about 118 is far above 22.5. Ten-year EPS growth (from $5.26 in 2015 to $13.22 in 2025) does pass.
summaries.thiel: MPC answers few of Thiel's seven questions well: it has no proprietary technology, operates in a crowded commodity market and does not ride a new secular trend. Its strength is durability of hard-to-replicate assets in an industry where no large new US refinery is being built, which gives it some of the monopoly-like benefit of efficient scale.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for durable compounders in big secular trends with good unit economics and fair prices, and MPC fits poorly: its revenue fell three years running to 2025 and its trend is a slowly declining fuel market. It is efficient and shareholder-friendly, and its free-cash-flow yield of about 9.6% is high, but much of that cash flow comes from a temporary margin spike.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller's focus on earnings momentum and catalysts fits MPC right now: earnings exploded in 2026 as the US-Iran conflict lifted crack spreads, analysts raised estimates and the stock is up about 160% in a year. The risk he would weigh is that the next 18-24 months probably look worse, with consensus projecting lower 2027 revenue and earnings as spreads normalize.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith avoids cyclical, capital-intensive businesses with low gross margins, and MPC's gross margin was about 10% in 2025 and its returns swing widely with the refining cycle. Management allocates capital sensibly through buybacks and MPLX growth, but it is not the kind of consistently high-return quality compounder Fundsmith buys.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula MPC looks decent today: trailing operating income of about $14,133M against an enterprise value near $161B gives an earnings yield of about 8.8%, and trailing ROIC is about 18%. Both figures are inflated by 2026's unusually wide crack spreads, so a normalized screen would rank it lower.
summaries.akre: Akre's three legs are a great business, talented and honest managers, and the ability to reinvest at high returns. MPC has competent, shareholder-aligned management, but refining is a commodity business without consistently high returns, and it reinvests little at high rates, returning most cash through buybacks instead.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai looks for simple businesses in temporary distress bought at a big discount, with low downside. MPC is simple and unlikely to fail, but it is at a cyclical high rather than in distress, and at $478.07 (above the $442 average analyst target) there is no Dhandho-style margin of safety.
summaries.wood: MPC does not fit ARK's disruptive-innovation framework: it refines fossil fuels, a market that electric vehicles and energy storage threaten to shrink. Its renewable diesel and natural gas processing are incremental, not exponential innovation platforms.
summaries.ackman: Ackman wants simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with strong barriers to entry and low exposure to commodities. MPC is simple and cash-generative with hard-to-replicate assets, and MPLX's fees add predictability, but its earnings depend heavily on commodity crack spreads, which conflicts with his criteria.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's scale-economics-shared model requires passing scale savings to customers to build an ever-stronger moat, which MPC does not do; it prices at market and returns gains to shareholders. Its long-term position is unlikely to strengthen materially as US fuel demand plateaus.
summaries.valentine: Valentine sought huge, growing markets and products that solve painful new problems, so a mature fuel refiner is far outside his approach. The market is large, but it is not growing or being created, and there is no technology-driven disruption in MPC's favour.
summaries.nash: MPC fails Nash's process at several steps: it is a commodity processor, consolidated debt of $32,816M exceeds cash of $7,768M, trailing operating margin is about 9%, and revenue fell from 2022 to 2025 before the 2026 spike. Momentum, buybacks and earnings beats are strong, but its Nash score totals about 70 and the 12% DCF value is far below the price.

momentum.evidence: Shares closed at $478.07 on Oct 16, 2026, up about 160% over 52 weeks and from about $248 in April 2026, far ahead of the market.

g4.evidence: CEO Maryann Mannen has executed well (Q2 2026 EPS of $17.73), and activist Elliott Management pushed earlier for the 2021 Speedway sale, but management is competent rather than legendary.

g6.evidence: The price is above the $442.33 average of 19 analysts' targets and 9 of 19 rate it Hold, suggesting many see the rally as priced in, though few call it outright overvalued.

simple.evidence: It buys crude, refines it into fuels at 13 refineries, sells them, and collects fees on MPLX pipelines and gas processing, a business any careful generalist can understand.

b2.evidence: Results swing with the refining cycle: net income attributable to MPC was a $9,826M loss in 2020, $14,516M in 2022 and $3,445M in 2024.

integrity.evidence: Management reports clearly, has used surplus cash to cut diluted shares from 649M (2020) to 290M (Q2 2026), and has a long-standing auditor (PwC) and a lead independent director.

b6.evidence: Rather than empire-building it sold Speedway in 2021 and returned most proceeds through buybacks, focusing capital on MPLX growth and existing refineries.

roic.evidence: Trailing ROIC is about 18% and ROE about 42%, but returns collapse in weak years (a loss in 2020) and leverage, mostly at MPLX ($25,640M of debt), boosts equity returns.

fcf.evidence: Free cash flow (operating cash flow minus capex) was positive in each year 2021-2025, e.g. $4,767M in 2025 against $4,047M of net income attributable to MPC, and about $12,899M over the last twelve months.

b10.evidence: Instead of retaining cash it bought back about half its shares since 2020, and the stock rose from about $59 (dividend-adjusted) in October 2021 to $478.07.

safety.evidence: At about 16.6x trailing EPS of $28.84, which is inflated by peak 2026 crack spreads, and above the average analyst target, the price offers no margin of safety on normalized earnings.

fairprice.evidence: About 7.5x 2026 consensus EPS of $63.34 looks cheap, but analysts expect earnings to fall in 2027 and 2028, so on normalized earnings the price is full.

mu5.evidence: Scale and irreplaceable assets make bankruptcy unlikely, but there are several ways to lose value: falling crack spreads, declining gasoline demand, refinery accidents and tighter regulation.

reinvest.evidence: MPC's 2026 capex outside MPLX is only $1.5B; it cannot reinvest most profits at high returns, so it returns them through buybacks and dividends.

ly2.evidence: It is a clear cyclical: earnings rise and fall with refining margins, as Q2 2026 R&M margin of $36.33/bbl versus $17.58 a year earlier shows.

ly3.evidence: Trailing P/E is about 16.6, while analysts expect earnings to decline after 2026 (Simply Wall St consensus earnings of $17,663M in 2026, $14,345M in 2027, $9,097M in 2028).

runway.evidence: US fuel demand is flat to declining and consensus revenue for 2028 ($154,655M) is below 2026's $171,706M estimate.

ly7.evidence: The company has shrunk diluted shares from 649M in 2020 to 290M in Q2 2026 (with $6.1B of buyback authorization left), but there is no evidence of notable insider buying; insiders own about 0.19%.

ly8.evidence: Refining is a 'boring' niche, but MPC is an S&P 500 company covered by about 19 analysts, so it is not overlooked.

fi2.evidence: It has added renewable diesel (Dickinson, 184 million gallons a year, and the Martinez JV with Neste) and is expanding MPLX gas processing, but its core products are unchanged.

fi3.evidence: MPC does not report meaningful R&D spending, so its R&D results cannot be judged.

fi4.evidence: Its brand and wholesale network supplies 7,882 Marathon jobber outlets and 1,162 ARCO dealer sites, but selling a commodity relies on logistics more than salesmanship.

longterm.evidence: Management funds long-life MPLX projects (2026 growth capex raised to $2.9B) but prioritises capital return and near-term cash generation over innovation.

gr1.evidence: It is the largest US refiner with $132,699M of 2025 sales and a market value of about $134B.

ni10.evidence: It lost $9,826M (net income attributable to MPC) in 2020, so it was not profitable in each of the last ten years.

gr4.evidence: MPC became an independent public company in its 2011 spin-off from Marathon Oil, so it has paid dividends for only about 15 years.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $5.26 in 2015 to $13.22 in 2025, about 2.5 times.

gr6.evidence: The $478.07 price is about 30.6 times average 2023-2025 diluted EPS of $15.64.

gr7.evidence: Trailing P/E of about 16.6 times P/B of about 7.1 gives roughly 118, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Refining uses widely available technology; MPC has no proprietary technology ten times better than rivals'.

timing.evidence: Near-term timing is favourable as the 2026 Middle East supply shock widened crack spreads, but the long-term trend toward electric vehicles works against fuel demand.

th3.evidence: MPC is an established leader in a large mature market, not a company that dominated a small niche and is expanding from it.

team.evidence: Management under Maryann Mannen executes well operationally and financially, but it is a professional team rather than an exceptional founder.
